h: Six Storeys of Old Town Life
p: Gladstone's Land rises six storeys above the Lawnmarket, which was typical of the Old Town, where space inside the city walls was so tight that people simply built upwards. Families of very different means lived stacked on top of each other, with the wealthiest often on the middle floors, away from the street smells below and the long climb to the top. Think about that as you walk round: your neighbours could be a merchant, a lawyer or a struggling tradesman.

At street level, look for the arcaded front. Arcaded shopfronts like this were once common along the Royal Mile, and here you can still see how goods would have been laid out for passers-by. It's one of the last survivors of its kind on the street, and it helps you picture the busy, noisy market that once filled the Lawnmarket.

The house has had a fair bit of care in recent years, with the National Trust for Scotland reopening it after a big refurbishment. The ice cream parlour on the ground floor has become a popular stop in its own right.

Allow around an hour. Visit early if you can, as the Royal Mile gets very busy, especially during the Festival in August. Afterwards, duck into Lady Stair's Close just next door to find the Writers' Museum, celebrating Burns, Scott and Stevenson. It's free and pairs perfectly with a visit here. The castle esplanade is a few minutes uphill, and the Scottish Parliament and Holyrood sit at the far end of the Mile.
